metaDescription: Six hose end garden sprayers compared on how they meter concentrate, dilution dial versus fixed ratio, tank size and cleaning, for lawns, shrubs and beds.
expertTake: The Ortho Dial N Spray is the best all round hose end sprayer because its dilution dial lets you follow a label rate for different products. The Chapin G390 is the value pick for fertilizer, a simple bottle with a fingertip valve. Skip hose end sprayers if your tap pressure is weak or you spray plants that cannot take overspray, since the ratio and the wet pattern depend on the hose.
introParagraphs: A hose end sprayer has no pump and no motor. Water from the garden hose rushes past a small orifice, and that flow pulls concentrate up from the bottle and blends it into the stream, in the same way a venturi works in a carburetor.

That elegance explains both the strengths and the limits. The sprayer is light, cheap and tireless, but its mixing ratio is set by the head and nudged by hose pressure. Choosing a good one is about the head design, bottle size and how easy it is to flush.

products.name: Ortho Dial N Spray Hose End Sprayer, 14 dilution settings

specList.label: Uses
specList.value: Liquid weed and insect killer, fungicide, fertilizer

products.description:
A dial turns the venturi into something you can adjust. Fourteen dilution settings let you match the head to the label rate of a particular product, so the same bottle can feed a lawn on one day and carry an insecticide the next. Three spray patterns give you a broadcast spray for turf and narrower options for beds.

The ergonomic design is meant to reduce strain on a long lawn pass, and the listing stresses precise application of liquid concentrates. Among the six it has the clearest ratio control, which is its edge over the fixed ratio bottles. Against the Chapin G390 it costs a bit more and adds the dial.

A dial is only as accurate as the water behind it. Hose pressure, the thickness of the concentrate and your walking pace all move the real ratio, so treat the settings as a close guide. Flush after each use and rotate the dial while water runs, since dried concentrate gums the dial passage. Dedicate separate bottles if you use weed killer. A practical test is to run plain water through it at your usual tap pressure and time how long a full bottle takes to empty, then compare that to the coverage on your product label, which tells you whether your hose delivers the flow the dial was designed around.
products.bestFor: Gardeners who feed, spray and treat with several different liquid products.
pros: Works with several liquid product types
cons: Real ratio varies with hose pressure
Dial passage clogs if not flushed

products.name: Chapin G390 32 Ounce Hose End Sprayer for Fertilizer
products.description:
This is the plain bottle at the low end of the cost range. A 32 ounce chemical resistant poly tank sits under a head with a metering orifice, a fingertip control starts and stops the flow, and a universal fit connects it to a standard hose. An optional Chapin quick connect accessory makes changing between hose tools quicker.

It has no dial, so the ratio comes from the head and you choose your product accordingly. That simplicity means fewer passages to clog and a bottle that is easy to flush. For water soluble fertilizer and similar liquids it is a good fit, and it is the pick when you spray the same thing season after season.

Compared with the Ortho it costs less and holds the same volume, and compared with the Chapin G385 insecticide bottle it is built for feeding. Flush after each use, store it with the cap off and replace the hose washer when it cracks. Because the head has no moving dial, a blocked orifice is the only common failure, and a few minutes in warm water with a soft brush usually clears it. If you notice the spray reaching only a few feet, check the pickup tube for a kink or a crust before you assume the head is worn.
products.bestFor: Feeding lawns and beds with the same product on a regular schedule.
pros: Simple head with few passages to clog
Universal hose fit with quick connect option
Lowest price tier in the lineup

products.name: RL Flo-Master Chameleon 32 Ounce Hose End Sprayer
products.description:
The Chameleon's special feature is its three pattern head: a fan for broad areas, a shower for delicate foliage and a stream for high places. Since hose end sprayers take their strength from the hose, the pattern selector is how you tailor the spray without changing the head.

The listing notes that it keeps direct contact with the chemical to a minimum, which is a safety point because concentrate is the part you least want on skin. The bottle is 32 ounces, and the label covers fertilizers, weed killers, fungicides and insect killers. Against the Ortho it offers more patterns but no dilution dial.

Plan on dedicated bottles if you spray herbicide, because residues in the head are hard to purge. Flush the pattern collar as well as the bottle after every use, and keep the cap off in storage. The three pattern collar turns on a small O ring, so a smear of silicone grease once a season keeps the shower and stream positions from sticking. Never force the collar past a stop, since a split ring will leak onto your hand.
products.bestFor: Gardens with a mix of turf, shrubs and tall plants.
pros: Fan, shower and stream in one head
cons: Share with herbicide at your peril

products.name: Nature's Wisdom Multi Use Hose End Sprayer 32 oz, 2 pack
products.description:
Two refillable bottles in the pack suit a gardener who wants to dedicate one to each product. Each has a K1 spray head with a 30 to 1 mixing ratio, meaning roughly thirty parts water to one of concentrate, which is a considerably stronger mix than a 100 to 1 head and suits products that call for more than a trace.

The listing positions it as a multi use sprayer for windows, high places, pesticides and washing as well as garden use. The bottles arrive empty, so you choose the product. With a fixed ratio there is no dial to get wrong, which is the point for a person who follows a single label.

As with all hose end heads, rinse the head after every use and avoid leaving concentrate in the bottle. Because both bottles are identical, write the product name on each with a permanent marker, and stand them on different shelves so you never reach for the wrong one while the hose is already running. Put beside the Chapin G385 it offers a stronger stated ratio, and compared with the Ortho it removes the adjustment.
products.bestFor: People who want two dedicated bottles and a stronger fixed ratio.
pros: Simple K1 head with no dial

products.name: Chapin G385 32 Ounce Insecticide Hose End Sprayer, fan nozzle
products.description:
This bottle is built for pest products, and the detail that matters is the fan nozzle. A flat fan lays insecticide across foliage in an even sheet, rather than a cone that leaves bare gaps between passes. The listing says one fill sprays about six gallons of finished mix, which is a handy number: it tells you how much area a bottle of concentrate will treat before you need to refill.

A 32 ounce chemical resistant poly tank handles water soluble pesticides and lawn chemicals, and a universal fit connects to a standard garden hose. An optional quick connect accessory speeds up switching between a nozzle and the sprayer. Compared with the Chapin G390 it is the pest oriented sibling with a fan pattern, and compared with the Chameleon it has fewer patterns but a plainer, cheaper head.

Keep it as a dedicated pest control bottle: label it, flush it after each use with clean water and store it with the cap off. Spray in the cool of the day, and keep the hose pressure moderate so the mix does not blow past the target leaf.
products.bestFor: Treating foliage for insects and lawn pests with an even fan pattern.
pros: Flat fan nozzle for even foliage coverage

buyingCriteria.criterion: How the venturi sets the ratio
buyingCriteria.explanation: A hose end head draws concentrate by water flow, so the ratio is a property of the head and the flow. The Ortho Dial N Spray adjusts it with 14 settings, while the Chapin G390 and Nature's Wisdom use fixed heads. If you spray more than one product, a dial saves guesswork. If you spray one product, a fixed head is simpler and has fewer passages to clog.

Concentrates are labelled with a rate, and your head must be able to meet it. The Nature's Wisdom delivers 30 to 1, while a very dilute head can deliver 100 to 1, a threefold difference in strength. Check the product label against the head before you pour, because an under dosed lawn feed does nothing and an over dosed one burns.

Low water pressure under doses the mix, while very high pressure can over dose it. A kinked or long hose changes flow too. Always run a short test with plain water to see how long a tank takes to empty, and compare it to the label coverage.

Hose end sprayers deliver a wet, broadcast pattern. The Chameleon offers fan, shower and stream and the Ortho offers three patterns, which is better than a single fixed cone. A broad fan is right for lawns and a narrow stream for high branches.

A 32 ounce bottle treats a reasonable chunk of lawn, while the Chapin G385 is sized to spray about six gallons per fill. A big bottle is heavy at the end of a hose, so match it to your yard. Measuring lines on the side help you mix the right amount.

A hose end sprayer should be used with a backflow preventer on the tap where required, so concentrate cannot siphon back into household water. Check your local rules, and keep the bottle upright while the water runs. Wear gloves when handling concentrate, and fill the bottle before you connect it so you are not pouring beside a live hose. After spraying, shut the tap first, then squeeze the head to bleed off the pressure before you unscrew the bottle.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ratio control
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared fixed heads with dial heads. The Ortho with 14 settings led on flexibility, and the Chapin G390 and K1 head bottles led on simplicity.

howWeEvaluated.title: Bottle design
howWeEvaluated.description: Bottle size, material and measuring marks were reviewed. All five bottles hold 32 ounces, so we scored on material and on how clearly the listing describes what a fill will cover, where the Chapin G385 led with about six gallons per fill.

howWeEvaluated.title: Pattern options
howWeEvaluated.description: The Chameleon with three patterns and the Ortho with three scored highest. Single pattern K1 head bottles scored lower.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ease of cleaning
howWeEvaluated.description: Based on owner feedback patterns, blocked heads are the main complaint. Fewer passages and easy flushing scored higher.

howWeEvaluated.title: Value for dedicated use
howWeEvaluated.description: Two bottle packs allow one product per bottle, which prevents cross contamination. The Nature's Wisdom pack scored well on that basis.

cards.text: You can match the head to a label rate, which helps when you switch products. Pick: Ortho Dial N Spray.

cards.label: Fixed ratio heads
cards.text: Simpler and less likely to clog, but you must buy a product that fits the head. Picks: Chapin G390, Chapin G385, Nature's Wisdom and the Chameleon.

howToChoose.note: Choose a dial if you spray many products, and a fixed head if you spray one.

maintenance.task: Flush the head with clean water
maintenance.why: Concentrate dries in the metering orifice and blocks it. A flush keeps the venturi clear.

maintenance.task: Rotate the dial through all settings while rinsing
maintenance.why: A dial passage can seize when residue dries. Moving it keeps it free.
A cracked washer leaks at the tap. It costs little and takes a minute.
Mixing up a herbicide bottle and a feed bottle can damage a lawn.

maintenance.task: Store dry with the cap off
maintenance.why: A damp closed bottle grows mildew and blocks the pickup tube.

faq.q: How does a hose end sprayer work?
faq.a: Water flows through the head and pulls concentrate from the bottle by suction, then mixes it. The ratio depends on the head and the water flow.
They are accurate enough for lawns if you follow the label, but the real ratio varies with pressure. For exact doses use a pump sprayer with a measured batch.

faq.q: Do I need a backflow preventer?
faq.a: Many places require one on the tap so that concentrate cannot siphon back into household water. Check your local rules, since a simple screw on backflow device is cheap and takes seconds to fit.

faq.q: What does a ratio such as 30 to 1 mean?
faq.a: It means thirty parts of water to one part of concentrate, and a larger first number gives a weaker mix. Make sure your label rate matches the head, and if the label asks for a stronger dose than the head delivers, use a pump tank and mix the batch by hand.

faq.q: Why does my sprayer stop pulling liquid?
faq.a: The pickup tube or metering orifice is usually blocked by dried concentrate. Soak the head in warm water and clear the tube, then run clear water through it with the tap on low to check that it draws again. If it still does not pull, look for a missing or flattened pickup tube washer.

faq.q: Can I use one bottle for different products?
faq.a: It is safer to dedicate bottles. Residues can harm plants later, so use a two bottle pack.
